transcript.content: Hello. Welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Lately I’ve been overwhelmed by guilt about letting everyone down at home and at work, even when people tell me it’s not that bad. I just feel like I'm constantly failing everyone around me, and the pressure has become too much to handle on my own.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings of guilt and pressure, and have you ever had a similar period in your life before?

This current heavy feeling and guilt have been dragging on for about five months now. Looking back, I’ve actually had these cycles of feeling overly revved up for a few weeks and then sinking into these long, drained periods on and off for at least a few years, but they've become much more noticeable lately.
During those times when you felt "revved up," did you experience symptoms like needing much less sleep, racing thoughts, or taking unusual risks, and did they ever cause major problems in your life?

Yes, during those high-energy phases I only slept about four hours a night but woke up feeling wired, and my thoughts would race so fast I couldn't keep up with them. While I didn't take dangerous physical risks, I impulsively overcommitted to way too many projects and events. It caused real problems because of the inconsistency; my daughter even told me she never knew which version of me she was coming home to.

During those highly energized periods, did it ever get to the point where you needed to be hospitalized, or did you experience things like hearing voices or having beliefs that others found highly unusual?

No, it never got to the point of needing hospitalization, and I've never heard voices or lost touch with reality. While I did have moments of feeling incredibly confident—like thinking I was the only one who could truly turn things around at work—it never went beyond that kind of overconfidence.
How is this current low period affecting your daily life—are you still managing to work and handle your responsibilities, or has it become almost impossible to function?

It’s been incredibly hard to function, and I feel so guilty because I'm barely keeping my head above water. I've started missing deadlines and forgetting meetings, leaving my team at work to quietly pick up my slack. I'm also constantly backing out of plans with friends, and my daughter recently told me she just doesn't know which version of me she is going to get.
During this difficult low period, have you had any thoughts of self-harm or ending your life, or do you feel completely hopeless about the future?

No, I haven't had any thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life. But I do feel incredibly exhausted and heavy, and I'm just constantly overwhelmed by this intense guilt that I'm letting everyone down.
During those high-energy periods, did you ever engage in highly reckless behaviors that caused severe consequences, like spending sprees you couldn't afford, risky sexual behaviors, or legal trouble?

No, I’ve never had any severe consequences like reckless spending, risky sexual behavior, or legal trouble during those high-energy phases. Instead, my impulsivity mostly showed up as overcommitting to work projects, committees, and community events that I couldn't actually sustain once the energy wore off.

latest_inference.note: The patient describes a history of recurrent hypomanic episodes (characterized by decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, overconfidence, and increased goal-directed activity/overcommitting, without psychosis, hospitalization, or severe social/occupational impairment) and a current major depressive episode lasting five months with significant functional impairment. This clinical picture is diagnostic of Bipolar II disorder, which is coded as F31.8 under ICD-10. Since there is no history of manic episodes, Bipolar I depressive episodes (F31.3, F31.4) are ruled out.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's clinical presentation is highly characteristic of Bipolar II disorder (classified under F31.8 in ICD-10). They describe a current major depressive episode lasting five months, characterized by profound guilt, fatigue, and functional impairment. They also report a history of recurrent hypomanic episodes lasting a few weeks, characterized by a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, inflated self-esteem (overconfidence), and increased goal-directed activity (overcommitting to projects). There is no history of manic episodes, hospitalization, or psychotic symptoms, which rules out Bipolar I disorder.
